Tutorial
Guided tour of key features
Help
  1. Write or load a DDL definition in the top-left panel
  2. Select a Volume / Subvolume / DDL in the tree to set the parse scope
  3. Paste or drop a message or file capture (NETARD / FUP COPY) in the Data Input panel
  4. Click ▶ Parse — results appear in the bottom panels

Keyboard shortcuts:
  • ← → navigate previous / next message
  • ↑ ↓ move selection up / down in Parse Results
  • Esc closes any open modal, context menu, or search field
* comment line

48   LLLVAR 999 "Additional Data"

Lines starting with * are comments.

  • Scope path — the header shows the active Vol / SV / DDL; selecting a node in the tree sets the parse scope
  • Search bar — type to find fields; use < > to step through matches (Enter / Esc to clear); matching lines are highlighted in the editor
  • Save — stores the current editor content into the selected tree node; enabled only when content has changed
  • Clear — wipes the editor
  • Copy (⎘) — copies all DDL content to the clipboard as plain text
  • Drag & drop — drop a DDL text file onto the editor to preview it, then click Save to store it in the tree
  • Validation bar — appears below the editor; shows errors, warnings, and unresolved TYPE references with < > navigation and a copy button
  • Tree nodes show ✖ / ⚠ badges for errors and warnings; a Missing References section appears automatically for unresolved TYPEs
  • Filter box — type to narrow volumes / subvolumes / DDLs by name; Esc to clear
  • Click a chevron to expand or collapse a Volume or Subvolume
  • Click a DDL name to set it as the active parse scope (highlighted in accent color)
  • Right-click empty area → New Volume / Import… / Export All…
  • Right-click Volume → New Subvolume / Rename / Copy / Paste / Export… / Delete
  • Right-click Subvolume → New DDL / Rename / Copy / Paste / Export… / Delete
  • Right-click DDL → Rename / Copy / Export… / Delete
  • Drop a .json export file onto the tree pane to import it directly
  • Paste one or more messages — separate them with a blank line
  • Format auto-detect — the parser automatically identifies the input format (Pure Hex, Spaced Hex, HexAscii, ASCII, NETARD, etc.) on each parse
  • Format selector (Auto dropdown) — override auto-detection by selecting a specific format; the dropdown turns amber when a format is forced
  • ISO timestamp prefixes (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS) are automatically stripped and displayed separately
  • NETARD capture files are supported (multi-record, multi-message); a Line Width control appears in the header for NETARD input
  • Files parse too — paste or drop a FUP COPY capture ($VOL.SUBVOL.FILE  RECORD n headers); each record is split out and parsed like a message, matched against File detection types by its wrapper filename
  • Drop any text or capture file onto the panel to load it
  • ✕ Clear button — clears all input and resets the parser
  • Use < > arrows in the header to navigate between messages when multiple are loaded
  • The header shows a format badge (e.g. NETARD, HEX) and a message count badge when multiple messages are present

Detection is configurable — for messages AND files. Open ⊞ Class Editor from the top bar to define message and file types. Each type carries an ordered list of recognizers — byte-level conditions such as a literal at an offset, an mti pattern, min-length/max-length, a numeric/regex field, a bitmap, or a source/destination/filename match.

  • All recognizers of a type must pass for it to match (first failing one short-circuits).
  • Types are tried in sidebar order; the first whose recognizers all pass wins.
  • File types (kind file) match FUP COPY records by their wrapper filename ($VOL.SUBVOL.FILE) via the filename recognizer; records without a wrapper filename never consult them, so they can't shadow message types.
  • Each type can also carry DDL bindings, a parse spec, a DE map, and field overrides.
  • Built-in defaults cover ISO 8583, STM, PSTM, Base24, NDC and a Segmented File template; edit or add your own. A message no type recognizes shows Unknown — click Data Detection in the results to define a rule.

When ▶ Parse runs:

  1. Manual override — a DDL is used for parsing only when you arm it: right-click the DDL or DEF in the tree and choose Use for parsing (override). The armed node turns amber with a ▶; right-click again (or arm another) to release it. Merely selecting a DDL does not arm anything, so a DDL open for editing never changes what Parse does. Arming is not remembered across reloads. While armed (single message, or a FUP COPY file capture), that DDL is used exclusively: no identification, no recognizers, no parse-spec run. The input is parsed strictly per the selected DDL, element by element, once. The USER badge shows in results and the progress overlay prints the amber Manual override mode — Identify · Recognizers · Parse-specs — not used notice.
  2. Detection → bound DDL. The recognizers run. If a type matches and it has a DDL binding, that bound DDL is used directly — compiled only if its content changed, then scored once. If the bound DDL scores below 95%, an amber ⚠ line flags it so you can verify the binding is right.
  3. DDL scoring. When nothing matches, or a matched type has no binding, candidate DDLs are compiled and scored. The score blends accuracy — per-byte type validity, with hard errors weighted 1.0 and soft type mismatches 0.7 — and coverage (bytes consumed ÷ message length), so a DDL that both fits the bytes and explains most of the message wins:
    • Zero → "No matching DDL for this message"
    • One → used automatically
    • Multiple → a picker lists each DDL and its score; you pick one for the session

The parse-progress overlay shows each step live — detection, any compilation (Compiling 1 of N), and scoring — so long DDL trees don't look frozen.

A segmented file's DEFINITION declares only SEGn TYPE xxx-SEG entries; the record on disk holds only the segments marked present by a 32-bit segment map (bit 0 = leftmost = SEG0, increasing left→right). The map can come from within the actual file or as an attribute on the parse-spec:

  • From the file — Base24 < 6.0: SEG0's header carries the live map (SEG-MAP, REDEFINES over SEG-MAP-R). Just name the field — it is read from the record at its DDL position:
    { "read-bitmap": { "field": "SEG-MAP" } }
  • From the file — Base24 6.0 IDF: the per-file SEG-MAP is zeroed and the real map is the IDF's FIID-SEG-MAP — also physically in the record:
    { "read-bitmap": { "field": "FIID-SEG-MAP" } }
  • On the parse-spec — Base24 6.0 non-IDF: the map is NOT in the record (it lives on the institution's IDF), so declare it with bits/value:
    { "read-bitmap": { "field": "FIID-SEG-MAP", "bits": 32, "value": "C4180000" } }
  • The SEG-MAP input at parse time overrides all of the above, ad-hoc (hex like C4180000 or 0/1 bits).
  • An all-zeros in-file map is the 6.0 signal "use the IDF map" — it is reported as an error, never silently read as empty.

A { "read-segment-fields": "…" } block then walks the DDL's top-level SEGn fields in declaration order, reading only the present segments (absent ones consume nothing). The map is shown at its true position in the results; leftover bytes after the last mapped segment are flagged. Tip: the bitmap Display override renders any field's raw bytes as 0/1 groups (C0400000 → 1100 0000 0100 0000 …).

Manual override on a segmented file walks the full DDL once (all segments assumed present) — type a map in the SEG-MAP bar to parse only the present segments.

The format is auto-detected on each parse. Separate multiple messages with one or more blank lines.

  • Pure hex — F0200022000000...
  • Spaced hex — F0 20 00 22 ...
  • Tandem dump — 0000: F0 F2 .. |0200|
  • ASCII raw — character bytes interpreted as-is
  • NETARD capture — multi-record files with packet headers; sub-formats (HEX, DUMP, OCT, EBCDIC, ASCII) are detected per-record
  • FUP COPY capture — file records with $VOL.SUBVOL.FILE  RECORD n headers (KEY n follows on a key-sequenced file and is absent on the rest) and hex or ASCII data lines — each record parses as a file record
  • Click a row → highlights that field's bytes in the Raw hex dump and selects it (accent background)
  • Hover a row → previews byte highlighting without changing selection
  • ↑ ↓ — move field selection up / down
  • Filter bar — type to narrow results by field ID or value
  • Columns dropdown — show or hide Field, Type / Description, Length, Value, Trk
  • Type / Description column — shows the field's DDL type (or HEADING). When a field has an override configured for its message type it reads declared ↩ override (same arrow the DDL uses for REDEFINES, e.g. TYPE BINARY 16 ↩ uint-be) plus as DISPLAY when a display override (amount, datetime, hex, ascii, ebcdic, gmt-ts, bitmap) is set — and the Value column shows the converted result.
  • Raw Hex column appears automatically when the Raw Message panel is collapsed
  • Drag any column header edge to resize that column
  • Hide Redef button — toggle visibility of REDEFINES fields
  • Trk checkbox — mark fields you want to track across messages
  • ⊞ Track Mode button — appears when at least one Trk checkbox is checked; switches to cross-message matrix view
  • ⬇ Export button — appears when messages are parsed; opens the message export modal
  • Double-click the panel title (e.g. Rec #975415) or the n / m counter to copy all fields of the current message to the clipboard as tab-separated text (Field ID, Description, Len, Value)
  • Double-click any field row to copy just that field to the clipboard
  1. Check Trk on any fields you want to compare
  2. Click ⊞ Track Mode in the Parse Results header
  3. A cross-message matrix appears — one row per tracked field, one column per message

  • Click ⊞ Track Mode again to return to the normal field list
  • Trk selections are preserved when navigating between messages

DDL Definitions:

  • Export — saves a .json file; choose exactly which Volumes / Subvolumes / DDLs to include via the checklist; can export a single DDL, an entire Subvolume, a Volume, or everything
  • Import — reads a previously exported .json; a preview modal shows conflicts before confirming
  • Drop a .json file onto the tree pane to import it directly

Messages:

  • ⬇ Export button in the Parse Results header — opens a modal to select and export parsed messages to a .json file with full field data and metadata
  • Drag any splitter bar to resize panels horizontally or vertically
  • Drag the right edge of the tree pane to resize it
  • Each panel has a − toggle button to collapse it to a labeled strip; click again to expand
  • At least one panel per row must remain expanded
  • Settings → Panels on Startup — set the default collapsed / expanded state for each panel at load time
  • All panel sizes, column widths, and column visibility are saved automatically in the browser
  • Go to Settings → Layout → ↺ Reset Layout to restore all defaults

Token maps link a 2-character token ID to the DDL name used to parse its data. Store them as DDL files inside the tree — the parser auto-detects them by their format.

Supported formats:

"B4" = EMV-STAT-TKN
EMV-STAT-TKN = "B4"
  • Both directions are accepted — "ID" = NAME and NAME = "ID"
  • Token IDs are exactly 2 characters enclosed in double-quotes
  • Comments (* in column 1) are ignored
  • If a token is not found in any map, the record is shown as unparsed (raw bytes with the token ID)
  • When the same token has both a Binary and an ASCII DDL variant (e.g. EMV-STAT-TKN and EMV-STAT-TKNX), map only the Binary name (without the X suffix) — the parser selects the X variant automatically for ISO/B24 messages
